documents.t: There are several ways to start, depending on how you like to work: In your browserBrowse, search, and publish nanopublications with Nanodash. Its templates mean you don't have to write RDF.On the command lineFetch, query, verify, and publish nanopublications with curl and the command-line tool. Follow the steps below.From codeUse a library for Java, Python, JavaScript, or Rust. There is a JavaScript example at the end of this page.With an AI agentAsk your coding agent to create, publish, and query nanopublications, using the nanopub Agent Skill. The steps below go from reading nanopublications to publishing your own. Steps 1 and 2 only need curl. Steps 3 and 4 use the command-line tool, which needs Java 21 or newer.

Every nanopublication has a resolvable URI. Ask for TriG and you get the RDF: curl -L -H "Accept: application/trig" \ https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo Open the same URI in a browser and you get a human-readable view in Nanodash. The examples page has more to try.
Published nanopublications are loaded into Nanopub Query instances. You can call ready-made queries through a REST API, or write your own SPARQL.

Each API endpoint runs a query that is itself published as a nanopublication. The endpoint URL is that nanopublication's ID plus the query name, and the placeholders in the query become URL parameters. This one is a full-text search: API=https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api curl -G $API/RAxdh5xkc6K6SMLY23yKu__zTWJPXeRFc0qgNNxkbOkpY/fulltext-search.csv \ --data-urlencode "query=Carabus granulatus" Nanopublications cannot be changed, so a new version is a new nanopublication that supersedes the old one. The announcement of Nano Session #29, for example, was edited several times. This query finds the latest version, starting from the first: API=https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api curl -G $API/RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I/get-latest-version-of-np.csv \ --data-urlencode "np=https://w3id.org/np/RAgITiAZA5yLltVB07D47Oo-kKVHOemwAkXnCq_ZYJtME" latest,date https://w3id.org/np/RAiODd0jLYxpvX3EHNpJfJr3mtcHgAo-QmYWoNYRqHvE0,2026-03-17T19:04:07.326Z The .csv suffix selects the result format, and .json works too. To see exactly what an endpoint does, fetch its definition like any other nanopublication: curl -L -H "Accept: application/trig" \ https://w3id.org/np/RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I Its assertion contains the SPARQL query, where the placeholder ?_np_iri becomes the np parameter. Because the definition is immutable too, an endpoint URL always runs the same query. This query lists all available ones.

The SPARQL endpoints cover all nanopublications. These are the five most recent ones: curl -G https://query.knowledgepixels.com/repo/full \ -H "Accept: text/csv" \ --data-urlencode 'query= PREFIX npa: <http://purl.org/nanopub/admin/> PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> SELECT ?np ?label ?date WHERE { GRAPH npa:graph { ?np dct:created ?date ; rdfs:label ?label . } } ORDER BY DESC(?date) LIMIT 5' The npa:graph graph holds metadata that the query service adds for each nanopublication, such as its label, its date, and the public key it was validly signed with. This query finds all nanopublications whose assertion mentions the beetle species, leaving out the ones that their authors retracted or superseded with a new version: curl -G https://query.knowledgepixels.com/repo/full \ -H "Accept: text/csv" \ --data-urlencode 'query= PREFIX np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> PREFIX npa: <http://purl.org/nanopub/admin/> PREFIX npx: <http://purl.org/nanopub/x/> PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> SELECT ?np ?label ?date WHERE { GRAPH ?assertion { ?s ?p <https://www.gbif.org/species/1036789> } GRAPH npa:graph { ?np np:hasAssertion ?assertion ; rdfs:label ?label ; dct:created ?date ; npa:hasValidSignatureForPublicKey ?pubkey . FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?newer npx:invalidates ?np ; npa:hasValidSignatureForPublicKey ?pubkey . } } }' To experiment, use the SPARQL editor in your browser.

Download the command-line tool of nanopub-java from Maven Central: V=$(curl -s https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/nanopub/nanopub/maven-metadata.xml \ | sed -n 's:.*<release>\(.*\)</release>.*:\1:p') curl -L -o nanopub.jar \ https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/nanopub/nanopub/$V/nanopub-$V-jar-with-dependencies.jar alias np='java -jar nanopub.jar' Save the beetle nanopublication and check it: curl -sL -H "Accept: application/trig" -o beetle.trig \ https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo np check beetle.trig Summary: 1 trusty with signature; 1 nanopub with issues "Trusty with signature" means that the hash in the URI matches the content, and that the signature is valid. The issue is only a warning that the nanopublication was created more than an hour ago, which matters when you publish a new one (np check -v shows the details). Now change a single label and check again: sed 's/Linnaeus, 1758"/Linnaeus"/' beetle.trig > tampered.trig np check tampered.trig Looks like a trusty nanopub BUT VERIFICATION FAILED: https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo Summary: 1 valid (not trusty); 1 nanopub with issues

Create a key pair. It is written to ~/.nanopub/, and existing keys are never overwritten: np mkkeys Write a nanopublication. It uses a temporary URI, which signing replaces with the final, hash-based one: cat > hello.trig <<EOF @prefix this: <http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np001/> . @prefix sub: <http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np001/> . @prefix np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> . @prefix dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> . @prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> . @prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . @prefix orcid: <https://orcid.org/> . @prefix wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> . @prefix wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/> . sub:Head { this: a np:Nanopublication ; np:hasAssertion sub:assertion ; np:hasProvenance sub:provenance ; np:hasPublicationInfo sub:pubinfo . } sub:assertion { wd:Q148 wdt:P36 wd:Q956 . # China - capital - Beijing } sub:provenance { sub:assertion prov:wasAttributedTo orcid:0000-0002-1825-0097 . } sub:pubinfo { this: dct:created "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"^^xsd:dateTime ; dct:creator orcid:0000-0002-1825-0097 ; dct:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/> ; rdfs:label "The capital of China is Beijing" . } EOF Replace 0000-0002-1825-0097 with your own ORCID iD. This one belongs to Josiah Carberry, ORCID's fictional test researcher. Then sign the nanopublication and publish it to the test server: np sign -s https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097 -o hello.signed.trig hello.trig np publish -u https://test.registry.knowledgepixels.com/ hello.signed.trig grep '@prefix this:' hello.signed.trig The last line shows the trusty URI of your new nanopublication. publish may warn that no templates are declared. Templates only matter for how Nanodash displays and edits a nanopublication, so you can ignore this warning here. Two things to know before you publish on the live network, which is what publish does without -u: Nothing can be deleted. You can supersede a nanopublication with a new version, or retract it with np retract, but the original stays on the network. Your key has to be linked to you. A signature proves which key signed, not who owns the key. For your nanopublications to be attributed to your ORCID iD, you declare your key in an introduction nanopublication (example), which an already trusted user then endorses. Nanodash generates a key for you automatically, and shows you how to publish the introduction.

The same steps in JavaScript with nanopub-js (npm install @nanopub/nanopub-js): import { Nanopub, NanopubClient } from '@nanopub/nanopub-js'; import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'; import { homedir } from 'node:os'; // Fetch and search const client = new NanopubClient(); console.log(await client.fetchNanopub( 'https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo')); for await (const row of client.findNanopubsWithText('Carabus granulatus')) { console.log(row.np, row.label); } // Run a ready-made query for await (const row of client.runQueryTemplate( 'RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I/get-latest-version-of-np', { np: 'https://w3id.org/np/RAgITiAZA5yLltVB07D47Oo-kKVHOemwAkXnCq_ZYJtME' }, )) { console.log(row.latest, row.date); } // Sign and publish to the test server const np = Nanopub.fromRdf(readFileSync('hello.trig', 'utf8'), 'trig', { privateKey: readFileSync(`${homedir()}/.nanopub/id_rsa`, 'utf8'), orcid: 'https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097', }); await np.sign(); const { uri } = await np.publish('https://test.registry.knowledgepixels.com/np/'); console.log(uri); There are also libraries for Python, Java, and Rust, listed under Tools.

Read the guidelines for the formal structure of nanopublications. See how the network fits together in the technical architecture. Create nanopublications from templates in your browser with Nanodash. Let an AI coding agent do all of the above with the nanopub Agent Skill. Ask questions in the Matrix channel.

This is an incomplete list of systems that use nanopublications. If you know of one that is missing, let us know. Knowledge Collaboratory: annotate biomedical claims, publish the annotations as nanopublications, and browse nanopublications. Data Stewardship Wizard: publish FAIR implementation profiles as nanopublications. RiverBench: a benchmark suite for RDF systems, where users publish their benchmark results as nanopublications. RDF Stream Taxonomy (RDF-STaX): a living literature review of RDF streaming, maintained as nanopublications. fairworkflows: a Python library for constructing, modifying, and publishing scientific workflows described with semantic technologies.
Nanopublications are published in a decentralized network of services and applications. All components are open source, and the core services run as multiple instances.

A client, such as Nanodash, a library, or the command-line tool, creates a nanopublication, signs it, and sends it to any Nanopub Registry. The registries replicate nanopublications among each other. Nanopub Query instances load the nanopublications from a registry into triple stores. They offer SPARQL endpoints over all nanopublications, as well as over subsets such as a single type, a single public key, or the last 30 days. They also offer a REST API whose queries are themselves published as nanopublications. Nanodash and other applications read through Nanopub Query and publish through the registries. Because nanopublications are immutable and identified by hashes, any copy can be checked against its URI, no matter which instance served it.

Nanopub Registry (instance, code) is the second-generation service for publishing and retrieving nanopublications in a decentralized fashion. Nanopub Query (instance, code) is the second-generation service to query nanopublications. It allows for decentrally querying the published nanopublications via a number of SPARQL endpoints covering different subsets and aspects of nanopublications. Nanodash (instance, code) is a general client and user interface for nanopublications. It allows for user-friendly browsing, querying, and publishing of nanopublications, but can also be used as an API and intermediary layer for other services to build upon. The legacy nanopub-server (instance, code) still holds the old (unsigned) nanopublications, but otherwise no longer has a function in the latest generation of the ecosystem.

Nanopub Monitor (instance, code) observes the services that run the core components of the ecosystem. Vodex (code) is a vocabulary index service, used to provide auto-complete on third-party vocabularies. nanopub-http (code) provides features of the nanopublication libraries over HTTP, most importantly signing and publishing.

These are published nanopublications. Each link opens a readable view in your browser. To get the RDF instead, request the same URI with Accept: application/trig, as shown in the quick start.

RAlohixCBW links a species of ground beetle to a habitat type. RAjcIFuVe7 states a scientific claim as an AIDA sentence and links it to more specific claims. RACK9s48ZO expresses a testable hypothesis in developmental biology, together with a proposed test. RAn4ChpN8n formulates a research question in the PICO format (population, intervention, comparison, outcome). RA2hQWbV8l introduces and defines a new concept ("generalist registry"). RAV_-_t50g defines a scientific variable as a FAIR Digital Object (FDO), following the I-ADOPT framework.

RAsyWOaZ7W states how three papers cite a given paper, with typed citations (CiTO). RAkDzG4wAG highlights a passage of a scientific article and comments on it. RAbp6LX5SR states that the creator has read a particular paper. RACEKjxyGN declares that the creator participates in a conference.

The nanopublication ecosystem is described in nanopublications too: users and their keys, the templates for creating nanopublications, the queries behind the API, and retractions. RASg5YBHps introduces a user and declares the public key they sign their nanopublications with. RALC35Q-V7 defines a template, from which nanopublications like the AIDA sentence above are created. RATC_tCEzO defines a SPARQL query, which is then available as an API. RAVa2aRzyu declares the retraction of another nanopublication.
The Nanopublication Guidelines specify the minimal formal structure of a nanopublication, and the Nanopublication Schema defines its vocabulary in RDF. This page summarizes them.

A nanopublication is a set of RDF quads in four named graphs: The assertion graph holds the main content. The provenance graph says how the assertion came to be, and must refer to the assertion graph. The publication info graph has metadata about the nanopublication as a whole, such as its creator and creation time, and must refer to the nanopublication. The head graph ties the three together and identifies the nanopublication. This is a minimal nanopublication in TriG, the recommended syntax: @prefix : <http://example.org/pub1/> . @prefix ex: <http://example.org/> . @prefix np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> . @prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . @prefix dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> . @prefix orcid: <https://orcid.org/> . :Head { : a np:Nanopublication . : np:hasAssertion :assertion . : np:hasProvenance :provenance . : np:hasPublicationInfo :pubinfo . } :assertion { ex:trastuzumab ex:is-indicated-for ex:breast-cancer . } :provenance { :assertion prov:wasDerivedFrom :experiment . :assertion prov:wasAttributedTo orcid:0000-0003-3934-0072 . } :pubinfo { : dct:creator orcid:0000-0003-0183-6910 . : dct:created "2020-07-10T10:20:22.382+02:00"^^xsd:dateTime . }

A nanopublication is well-formed if: every triple is in one of the four graphs, and every graph has a URI; the head graph contains exactly one rdf:type np:Nanopublication triple, which identifies the nanopublication URI; the head graph links the nanopublication to exactly one assertion, one provenance, and one publication info graph; the URIs of the nanopublication and its four graphs are all different; the provenance graph refers to the assertion graph at least once, and the publication info graph refers to the nanopublication at least once.

Nanopublications are immutable, and their identifiers make this checkable. The recommended way is a Trusty URI: a URI that ends in a cryptographic hash of the nanopublication's content, like RAlohixCBW... in this example. Anyone who has the content can recompute the hash and check that it matches. The URIs of the graphs and of other resources the nanopublication defines are derived from its URI, so they are fixed by the hash too.

In the current ecosystem, nanopublications are also signed. The publication info graph then contains the creator's public key and a signature, and the trusty URI is computed over the signed content. The quick start shows how to sign, verify, and publish nanopublications.

Examples of published nanopublications Tools to create and process nanopublications A Robust Decentralized Infrastructure for Trust-Aware Open Knowledge Sharing (ISWC 2026), the paper on the nanopublication ecosystem
These tools let you create, publish, and query nanopublications. The quick start shows the command-line tool and the JavaScript library in action.

Nanodash (code) is a web interface for browsing, searching, and publishing nanopublications, with templates that make it easy to create them without writing RDF. The Knowledge Collaboratory helps annotate biomedical text, publish those annotations as nanopublications, and browse them.

The nanopub-java release jar is also a command-line tool, with commands such as check, sign, publish, retract, query, and mkkeys: java -jar nanopub-<version>-jar-with-dependencies.jar check my-nanopub.trig The jar is on Maven Central, and the quick start shows how to download the latest one.

Language Library Install Java nanopub-java, the reference implementation Maven: org.nanopub:nanopub Python nanopub-py pip install nanopub JavaScript / TypeScript nanopub-js, for Node.js and the browser npm install @nanopub/nanopub-js Rust nanopub-rs, with bindings for Python and JavaScript cargo add nanopub All of them can sign, verify, and publish nanopublications.

nanopub-skill is an Agent Skill that lets AI coding agents work with nanopublications in natural language: creating, signing, publishing, querying, superseding, and retracting them, as well as authoring templates, resource views, and Spaces. It follows the open Agent Skills format, and so works with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and many other agents.

More tools are in the Nanopublication and Knowledge Pixels GitHub organizations. Trusty URIs are the hash-based identifiers that nanopublications use. A Robust Decentralized Infrastructure for Trust-Aware Open Knowledge Sharing (ISWC 2026) is the paper on the nanopublication ecosystem: its services, network, and trust algorithm.

This tutorial took place on 2 June 2025 at ESWC 2025 in Portorož, Slovenia. See the program with schedule and materials.

Nanopublications are a rapidly growing technology, fully based on Semantic Web standards and principles. At this tutorial, participants are introduced to the concept and then immediately get hands-on experience in creating and publishing their own nanopublications as well as querying and using the available content. The tutorial covers how to create nanopublications manually via web forms and automatically via software libraries, how to retrieve published nanopublications from the decentralized network, how to craft own web forms via templates, how to query the network with SPARQL, and how trust and communities are handled. Moreover, participants get brief introductions into a selection of existing systems and approaches that are based on this technology. The attendees will get supervision and advice from the core people driving the nanopublication technology, and will have time during the tutorial to make some first concrete steps in applying it to their areas of interest. At the end, attendees will have a comprehensive basic foundation on the theory and practice of nanopublication technology.

The objective of this tutorial is to give attendees the skills needed to work with nanopublications, along with the knowledge on how they may be applied in scientific work. This tutorial will briefly cover the conceptual framework and motivation, and then focus on providing practical hands-on experience on the usage of nanopublications, covering the whole data lifecycle from creating nanopublications to connecting, querying, combining, and reusing them. This was the first nanopublication tutorial of this kind. Its material builds upon numerous presentations, seminar sessions, and publications we have authored on the topic, and is designed to be easy to update and reuse for further editions.

The target audience are Semantic Web researchers and developers, and generally anyone interested in the technical aspects of nanopublications. The learning goals are the following: Participants know the motivation and vision behind nanopublications Participants know the technical basis of nanopublications and how they relate to other semantic technologies Participants can create their own nanopublications, via the Nanodash user interface as well as programmatically Participants know how to publish and query nanopublications Participants know the basics of how to create their own nanopublication templates Participants understand how agents are identified and trusted on the decentralized nanopublication network Participants have made their first steps in using nanopublications for a small project of their choosing

The tutorial day included sessions on the following topics: What are nanopublications? Creating and publishing nanopublications Creating nanopublication templates Querying nanopublications Applications Trust and communities Individual projects The detailed schedule with the materials can be found here.

Tobias Kuhn is Assistant Professor at VU University Amsterdam, and more recently CTO at the start-up Knowledge Pixels. He is one of the main drivers behind the nanopublication technology and community, having published more than 15 peer-reviewed articles on nanopublications and having led the development of nanopublication software such as nanopub-java and Nanodash. He has also extensive experience with tutoring and lecturing, having organized and taught more than 30 courses at university level over the last 20 years on topics including knowledge organization and information retrieval.

Barbara Magagna is the FAIR Development and Fellowship Coordinator at GO FAIR Foundation (GFF) with a background in landscape ecology, GIS and semantics. She is trainer of the 3-Point FAIRification Framework, for which she developed core components. Nanopublications are at the core of GFF’s Capacity Building Programme leveraging the documentation of FAIR Supporting Resources. Within European projects (ENVRI, eLTER, PARC, FAIR2Adapt) she helps to assess FAIRness of data and services and to develop semantic frameworks (I-ADOPT).

Vincent Emonet is a senior researcher at the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB), specializing in semantic web technologies, data integration, and scientific knowledge representation. He has extensive experience in teaching and supervision, having co-organized numerous workshops and tutorials around the topics of the FAIR data principles in general and nanopublications in particular. Vincent is dedicated to empowering scientists with practical skills and tools for managing and sharing structured scientific knowledge. His work has led to many scientific papers on the topic and he has made significant contributions to fostering collaboration and reproducibility in the life sciences.

Piotr Sowiński is a PhD student at the Warsaw University of Technology and a co-founder of the start-up NeverBlink. His work revolves around the topics of Knowledge Graphs, streaming, and distributed systems. He is currently leading two community initiatives that use nanopublications: RiverBench (with structured reporting of RDF benchmarks), and the RDF Stream Taxonomy (with a living literature review of RDF streaming). He also contributes to the open source projects powering the nanopublication ecosystem. Since 2022 Piotr has been teaching hands-on classes about Knowledge Graphs for graduate students.
